# Debiased prior-data fitted networks

## Setting of the debiased PFNs {.smaller}

- We observe $\mathcal D_n=(W_1,\dots,W_n)$ with $W_i=(Y_i,D_i,X_i)$ from a law $P_0$. The target $\theta(P)$, for
  example the average treatment effect (ATE), has the efficient influence function $\varphi_P$ and the expansion
  $\theta(P)-\theta(P_0)=-P_0\varphi_P+R_2(P,P_0)$ with a remainder of second order.
- A prior-data fitted network (PFN) for $\theta$ is trained on data sets simulated from laws $P\sim\Pi$, with the log
  loss of its output density $q(\theta\mid\mathcal D_n)$ at the label $\theta(P)$ [@muller2022transformers].
  @melnychuk2026debiased call the network idealised when its output is the posterior of $\theta$ under $\Pi$.
- [Theorem 1 of the paper.]{.label} The error of the posterior of the target is bounded by the posterior average of the
  nuisance error plus the remainder. Under assumptions on where the posterior puts its mass, it concentrates no faster
  than the nuisance posteriors. For the ATE this first-order term is the error of the outcome regressions and the
  covariate law, and the authors read the theorem as a generalisation of the prior-induced bias
  [@hahn2018regularization; @melnychuk2026frequentist].

## Two corrections in pretraining {.smaller}

[Label correction.]{.label} The network is trained on the label
$$
\tilde\theta(P)=\theta(P)+\sum_{i=1}^n\varpi_i\,\varphi_P(W_i),\qquad(\varpi_1,\dots,\varpi_n)\sim\mathrm{Dirichlet}(1,\dots,1),
$$
with the influence function computed from the nuisances of the simulated law $P$. This moves the one-step posterior
correction of @yiu2025semiparametric into pretraining. For the ATE the label is a Bayesian bootstrap average of AIPW
pseudo-outcomes.

[Prior correction.]{.label} Each simulated law $P$ is perturbed along a least-favourable submodel, a one-dimensional
submodel through $P$ whose score is $\varphi_P$, with a coefficient $\lambda\sim N(0,\sigma_n^2)$ and
$n\sigma_n^2\to\infty$, which extends the prior correction of @ray2020semiparametric. For the ATE with Gaussian noise
of unit variance, the outcome regression $g$ becomes $g+\lambda\alpha$, with the Riesz representer
$\alpha(d,x)=d/m(x)-(1-d)/\{1-m(x)\}$, and the covariate law is reweighted.

In both cases the network keeps its interface. It returns the posterior of $\theta$ and no nuisances, so no correction
step runs at test time.

## Guarantees and their scope {.smaller}

- [Theorem 2.]{.label} With either correction, the posterior concentrates at the rate $n^{-1/2}$ plus the
  posterior average of the remainder, under a stochastic equicontinuity condition on the empirical term
  $(\mathbb P_n-P_0)(\varphi_P-\varphi_{P_0})$.
- [Theorem 3.]{.label} When the remainder is $o_P(n^{-1/2})$, a semiparametric Bernstein–von Mises theorem holds with
  the efficient variance, so credible intervals have an asymptotic frequentist reading.
- [Theorem 4.]{.label} The worst-case risk of the corrected posterior mean is of order $n^{-1}$ plus the squared rate of
  the remainder, which is the minimax rate when a matching lower bound holds.

Every theorem assumes the idealised network, a network trained for one fixed $n$, and a true law $P_0$ in the support
of the prior. The approximation error of a trained network is set aside.

# The planned contribution

## The open problem {.smaller}

- A trained network computes $\hat\theta_\chi(\mathcal D_n)=\hat\theta_\Pi(\mathcal D_n)+a_\chi(\mathcal D_n)$, the
  Bayes rule $\hat\theta_\Pi=\mathbb E_\Pi[\theta\mid\mathcal D_n]$ plus an amortisation error. The theorems concern
  $\hat\theta_\Pi$, and $a_\chi$ enters the estimate directly.
- Pretraining controls $a_\chi$ only on average under the prior, and on data sets that differ from those of pretraining,
  for example in $n$ or in the number of covariates, nothing bounds it.
- In double machine learning, Neyman orthogonality of the score guarantees that nuisance errors have no first-order
  effect on the estimate [@chernozhukov2018double]. A PFN has no score, so this property cannot be checked for it.

[Question.]{.label} When is an estimator without a score, in particular a trained in-context learner, first-order
insensitive to errors in the outcome regression, and how can we check this from the data and the trained network
alone?

## The idea: move the truth and watch the estimate {.smaller}

- Shift the outcome regression $g_0(d,x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid D=d,X=x]$ to $g_0+\delta h$ for a direction $h(d,x)$, for
  instance by adding $\delta h(D_i,X_i)$ to every outcome. By the Riesz representation theorem the ATE moves by
  $\delta\langle\alpha_0,h\rangle$.
- An estimator whose mean moves by the same amount keeps its bias along the shift. An estimator whose mean moves less
  acquires a bias of order $\delta$.
- In the partially linear model, a plug-in estimate with a ridge penalty on the covariates moves less along
  $\alpha_0$. The penalised covariate part of the fit absorbs only part of the shift along the treatment regression,
  and the treatment coefficient absorbs the rest, which is the regularisation-induced confounding of
  @hahn2018regularization.
- The condition needs only the map $\mathcal D_n\mapsto\hat\theta$, so it applies to a trained network, which has no
  score.

## First-order insensitivity {.smaller}

[Outcome shifts.]{.label} For a direction $h$ and $\delta\in\mathbb R$, let $P_{\delta h}$ be the law of
$(Y+\delta h(D,X),D,X)$. The bias of $\hat\theta$ along the shift is
$b_n(\delta;h)=\mathbb E_{\delta h}[\hat\theta]-\theta(P_{\delta h})$, with $\theta(P_{\delta h})=\theta_0+\delta\langle\alpha_0,h\rangle$.

[Definition.]{.label} The estimator $\hat\theta$ is first-order insensitive in the direction $h$ if
$\partial_\delta b_n(0;h)=0$, and asymptotically first-order insensitive over a class of directions if this
derivative tends to zero uniformly over the class.

- The condition is the derivative part of local asymptotic unbiasedness [@hirano2012impossibility], and it is stated
  at fixed $n$.
- The direction $\alpha_0$ is the least-favourable direction for the ATE in the outcome regression when the conditional
  variance of $Y$ is constant, and for the ATE with Gaussian noise of unit variance it is the direction along which the
  prior correction perturbs $g$.

## Implicit weights {.smaller}

[Definition.]{.label} For an estimator that is differentiable in the outcomes, the implicit weights are
$w_i=n\,\partial\hat\theta/\partial Y_i$. They describe how the estimate responds to each outcome.

[Proposition.]{.label} Under a domination condition on the derivative of $\delta\mapsto\hat\theta(Y_{1:n}+\delta h)$,
$$
\partial_\delta b_n(0;h)=\mathbb E\Big[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\,h(D_i,X_i)\Big]-\langle\alpha_0,h\rangle .
$$
The estimator is first-order insensitive in the direction $h$ exactly when its implicit weights balance $h$ in
expectation, and over a class of directions exactly when they act in expectation as $\alpha_0$.

- For inverse probability weighting with the true propensity score, $w_i=\alpha_0(D_i,X_i)$, and the estimator is
  insensitive in every direction.
- For estimators linear in the outcomes, the $w_i$ are the implied weights of @chattopadhyay2023implied and the outcome
  weights of @knaus2024weighted. For posterior means in multilevel regression and poststratification they are the
  locally equivalent weights of @giordano2026locally.

## Checking a trained network {.smaller}

- For a network, the implicit weights take one backward pass. For a network available only as a black box, finite
  differences in the outcomes give the derivative along a chosen direction.
- The sample imbalance
  $\hat\Delta(h)=n^{-1}\sum_iw_ih(D_i,X_i)-n^{-1}\sum_i\{h(1,X_i)-h(0,X_i)\}$ estimates the sensitivity, and for
  directions $h$ estimated from the data, such as a fitted propensity score or a fitted outcome regression, it can be
  computed without the truth.
- A network that standardises the outcomes with the context mean and standard deviation satisfies
  $\hat\theta(a+bY_{1:n})=b\,\hat\theta(Y_{1:n})$. By Euler's theorem, $\hat\theta=n^{-1}\sum_iw_iY_i$ and
  $n^{-1}\sum_iw_i=0$, so its error splits exactly into the imbalance $\hat\Delta(g_0)$, a sampling term of mean zero
  and a weighted noise term.
- [Open.]{.label} A test with a known level needs conditions under which the implicit weights of a nonlinear estimator
  concentrate.

## Bayes rules of in-context learners {.smaller}

- [Lemma.]{.label} Over all measurable maps, the squared pretraining loss for a label $T(\xi,\mathcal D_n)$ is
  minimised by $\mathbb E_\Pi[T\mid\mathcal D_n]$, the Bayes rule of the network.
- [Independent mechanisms.]{.label} If the prior draws the treatment mechanism independently of the covariate and
  outcome mechanisms, as the priors of CausalPFN and CausalFM do, the posterior does not involve the treatment
  likelihood, and the Bayes rule for the ATE is a Bayesian outcome regression [@li2023bayesian].
- [Corollary.]{.label} The Bayes rule uses the treatment mechanism only if the label depends on it or the prior couples
  it with the outcome mechanism. The label correction is an instance of the first case, and the prior correction of the
  second.
- [One-step labels.]{.label} Under independent mechanisms, the Bayes rule for the one-step label
  $n^{-1}\sum_i[\tau_\xi(X_i)+\alpha_\xi(Z_i)\{Y_i-g_\xi(Z_i)\}]$, the conditional mean of the label of the label
  correction, is the AIPW estimator at the posterior means of the nuisances [@antonelli2022causal; @zhang2026fluctuate].
  The nuisances are evaluated on the rows to which they were fitted, so the empirical process term has to be controlled
  without sample splitting [@chen2022debiased].

## Relation of the two works {.smaller}

| | Debiased PFNs | Planned contribution |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Question | which pretraining makes the posterior debiased | how to check whether a given estimator is debiased |
| Object | the idealised network | any map $\mathcal D_n\mapsto\hat\theta$, including a trained network |
| Criterion | rates and a Bernstein–von Mises theorem as $n\to\infty$ | first-order insensitivity at fixed $n$ |
| Tool | label and prior corrections | implicit weights from one backward pass |
| Role of the corrections | the method | objects to evaluate, analysed through their Bayes rules |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

By Theorems 2 to 4 the corrections debias the idealised network, and the criterion measures how far a trained network
attains this.

## Planned contribution {.smaller}

1. A criterion for estimators without a score, first-order insensitivity along shifts of the outcome regression, with
   its characterisation through implicit weights and its relation to local asymptotic unbiasedness.
2. A diagnostic from one backward pass, the imbalance of the implicit weights, with conditions under which it gives a
   test with a known level.
3. The Bayes rules of in-context learners under the label and prior corrections, and the conditions under which they
   use the treatment mechanism.
4. The measurement of trained causal PFNs with this criterion, among them debiased PFNs with and without their
   corrections and networks with in-context nuisances, cross-fitting and an AIPW layer.

[Points for discussion.]{.label} Shifts of the treatment mechanism and of the covariate law, the empirical process term
without sample splitting, and the access to trained debiased PFNs.
